---
title: "TF24: hydraulics, and a fast acclimating variant"
---

::: {.eyebrow}
guide
:::

TF24 represents the movement of water from soil, through roots and stems, to
leaves. At each rate calculation it finds the root-collar water potential that
best balances two outcomes: opening stomata increases photosynthesis, but more
negative water potential increases hydraulic risk.

The standard TF24 model solves this optimisation from scratch each time. TF24f
("f" for fast or forecasting) instead carries the operating point forward and
allows it to adjust as conditions change. In practical terms, **TF24 repeatedly
finds the optimum, whereas TF24f tracks it**.

Tracking can reduce repeated calculations and also introduces a finite
acclimation time. This guide explains that approximation, compares the two
models, and shows the parameter that controls tracking speed.

```{r}
#| label: setup
library(plant)
library(plantpress)
library(dplyr)
library(tidyr)
library(ggplot2)

base <- function(type) {
  p <- base_parameters(type)
  p$hyperpar <- fieldtrial::tradeoffs(type)
  add_strategies(p, trait_matrix(0.0825, "lma"), birth_rate = 20)
}
```

## The idea: let the optimum chase a moving target

As a plant grows and its environment changes, the preferred operating point
moves. TF24f stores its current estimate as an extra state variable and adjusts
that state in the direction that increases carbon profit.

The state is not the collar potential itself. A collar potential is feasible
only between a wet end $a$, where no water flows, and a dry end $b$, where the
stem carries all it can, and both ends move as the soil wets and dries. So
TF24f stores the collar's relative position $u$ between them, as its logit
$z$, and the collar is $\psi = a + (b - a)\,u$. The state climbs the profit
gradient:

$$\frac{\mathrm{d}z}{\mathrm{d}t} = k \left[ (b - a)\,\frac{\partial\,\text{profit}}{\partial\psi} - 2\mu \sinh z \right].$$

At the optimum, the profit gradient is zero and the state stops moving. When the
optimum shifts, the gradient moves the state towards its new value. The gain
$k$ controls how quickly that adjustment occurs and therefore how much
acclimation lag remains. Every $z$ is a feasible collar, so the state can never
leave the bracket; the small barrier term $\mu$ stops it running on towards an
end where profit is still rising, and holds it a short step inside instead.

::: {.callout-note}
## How the gradient is calculated

`plant` calculates the gradient exactly with automatic differentiation and the
implicit-function theorem. In R, `k_acclim` controls the gain.
:::

## Run TF24 and TF24f side by side

The following example gives both models the same trait and recruitment inputs.
For TF24f we use an illustrative gain of 2; the package default is 1.

```{r}
#| label: run-both
tf24  <- tidy(run(base("TF24"), record = "steps"))

p_f <- base("TF24f")
s <- p_f$strategies[[1]]
s$k_acclim <- 2
p_f$strategies[[1]] <- s
tf24f <- tidy(run(p_f, record = "steps"))
```

In this example, the two size structures remain very similar:

```{r}
#| label: size-distributions
#| fig-alt: "Node height trajectories for TF24 and TF24f, which closely overlap."
bind_rows(
  tf24$species  |> drop_na() |> mutate(model = "TF24 (optimised)"),
  tf24f$species |> drop_na() |> mutate(model = "TF24f (tracked)")
) |>
  plot_size_distribution() +
  facet_wrap(~model) +
  coord_cartesian(expand = FALSE) +
  labs(title = "Same biology, two ways of resolving the leaf optimum")
```

TF24f records its tracked position in the state `collar_position`, a
dimensionless logit in which 0 is the middle of the bracket. Both models report
the collar potential in MPa as `opt_root_psi`, in the same positive-magnitude
convention: TF24's newly optimised value, and the potential TF24f's tracked
position implies. Plotting them together shows how closely the state tracks: at
this gain it lies on the optimum through the steep changes of the first years,
and the acclimation lag shows only where the optimum turns sharply, as near
year 25, before the two run close together again.

```{r}
#| label: tracking
#| fig-alt: "Tracked collar potential closely follows TF24's per-step optimum."
node1 <- function(d) d |> filter(node == 1) |> drop_na()
bind_rows(
  node1(tf24$species)  |> transmute(time, psi = opt_root_psi,       model = "TF24 optimum"),
  node1(tf24f$species) |> transmute(time, psi = opt_root_psi,       model = "TF24f tracked")
) |>
  ggplot(aes(time, psi, colour = model)) +
  geom_line() +
  labs(x = "Patch age (years)", y = "Root-collar potential (MPa)",
       colour = NULL, title = "The tracked state follows the moving optimum") +
  theme_classic()
```

## Choosing the gain `k`

A larger `k` makes the tracked state respond more quickly, but it also makes the
extra ODE state **stiffer**, which can force the adaptive solver to take many
smaller steps.
A smaller `k` is easier to integrate but produces a longer acclimation lag.
There is therefore no universal best value: compare TF24f against TF24 over the
environmental range and time scale relevant to the analysis.

The exact gradient avoids a finite-difference step and its truncation error,
so the gain is the only setting to choose.

## A note on initialisation

Each new seedling starts with its tracked state at the current optimum: TF24
solves the leaf once, and TF24f seats the seedling at that collar's position in
the bracket, kept a small margin from either end (an optimum on an end has no
finite logit). After initialisation, TF24f resumes tracking rather than
re-optimising at every step.

## Status

TF24f currently tracks the root-collar's position in its feasible bracket and
inherits TF24's selectable canopy models. It is an approximation with an explicit acclimation lag, not an
exact replacement for TF24.
